summary: This standards-track document specifies Mobile IPv6, which lets a node stay reachable while moving. A mobile node keeps a home address and gets a care-of address where it currently is. A home agent forwards traffic between them.

plainLanguage.summary: Your mail goes to your home address, and a helper forwards it to wherever you are staying, so friends always reach you.

questions: what is the return routability procedure
subtitle: How an IPv6 device keeps one permanent address and stays reachable while it moves from network to network.

tldr.problem: A device that changes networks normally has to change its IP address, which breaks the transport and application connections that were using the old address.
tldr.mechanism: A mobile node keeps a permanent home address and registers its current care-of address with a home agent on its home link. The home agent tunnels traffic to it, and correspondent nodes can learn the care-of address too and send packets straight to it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6275 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3775. It also defines the return routability procedure, which lets route optimization work without pre-arranged security associations.

today: RFC 6275 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3775. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Needs Mobility Support
sections.content:
Without specific mobility support in IPv6, packets for a mobile node cannot reach it once it leaves its home link. The node could take a new IP address on every new link, but then it could not keep transport and higher-layer connections alive when it changes location.

Mobile IPv6 solves this at the network layer. The mobile node keeps one home address, and movement stays transparent to transport protocols and applications. The protocol works across the same kind of medium (one Ethernet segment to another) and across different kinds (Ethernet to a wireless LAN cell).

The RFC is explicit about what it leaves out: links with unidirectional connectivity, access control on a visited link, local or hierarchical mobility management, assistance for adaptive applications, mobile routers, service discovery, and telling bit-error loss from congestion loss. It obsoletes RFC 3775, after problems were found during integration, testing and deployment of that earlier document.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move to a new house, your old address stops working for mail. This protocol lets you keep one permanent address so mail and calls keep finding you wherever you go.

sections.title: Home Address, Care-of Address and Binding
sections.content:
The home address is a unicast routable address assigned to the mobile node within its home subnet prefix. Standard routing delivers packets for it to the home link. While the node is away, it is also reachable at one or more care-of addresses, which carry the subnet prefix of the foreign link it is visiting. It can get them through conventional IPv6 mechanisms such as stateless or stateful autoconfiguration. The one registered with the home agent is the primary care-of address.

The association of a home address with a care-of address, plus the remaining lifetime, is a binding. A home agent is a router on the home link with which the mobile node has registered. Any peer the mobile node talks to is a correspondent node, and it may be stationary or mobile itself.

Three conceptual data structures keep track of this. The Binding Cache (kept by home agents and correspondent nodes) holds bindings for other nodes. The Binding Update List (kept by each mobile node) holds every binding the node has or is trying to establish. The Home Agents List records the other home agents on the same link.

Home and care-of addresses MUST be unicast routable addresses. Unique-local addresses SHOULD NOT be used as home or care-of addresses when other choices exist, because a node cannot always tell its home site from the site it is visiting.
sections.plainLanguage: Your home address is like your permanent street address. A care-of address is the hotel where you are staying this week, and a binding is the note that says which hotel goes with which home.

sections.title: Two Ways to Reach a Mobile Node
sections.content:
The RFC describes two modes of communication between a mobile node and a correspondent node.

In bidirectional tunneling, the correspondent node needs no Mobile IPv6 support and the mobile node does not have to have registered with it. Packets from the correspondent go to the home agent, which intercepts them using proxy Neighbor Discovery and tunnels them to the primary care-of address using IPv6 encapsulation (RFC 2473). Packets in the other direction are reverse tunneled to the home agent and then routed normally.

In route optimization, the mobile node registers its binding with the correspondent node. The correspondent then checks its cached bindings whenever it sends a packet. If it finds one, it sets the Destination Address to the care-of address and adds a new type of routing header carrying the home address. The mobile node, in turn, sets its Source Address to its care-of address and adds a Home Address destination option. This keeps the care-of address invisible above the network layer.

The RFC lists the benefits of the direct path: the shortest route, less congestion at the home agent and home link, and less impact from temporary failures of the home agent or of networks on the path to it.

Compared with Mobile IPv4, there are no special foreign agent routers, route optimization is a fundamental part of the protocol, and most packets use a routing header instead of encapsulation, which reduces overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Either your mail goes to your home first and a helper forwards it to you, or your friends learn where you are and mail you directly. The direct way is faster.

sections.title: The Mobility Header and Its Messages
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 defines a new IPv6 protocol, the Mobility Header, identified by Next Header value 135. It carries all messages used to create and manage bindings. Its fixed fields are Payload Proto, Header Len, MH Type, Reserved and a 16-bit Checksum, followed by type-specific message data. Implementations SHOULD set Payload Proto to IPPROTO_NONE (59), and the total length MUST be a multiple of 8 octets.

Eight message types exist (MH Type 0 to 7): Binding Refresh Request, Home Test Init, Care-of Test Init, Home Test, Care-of Test, Binding Update, Binding Acknowledgement and Binding Error. A receiver MUST ignore and skip mobility options it does not understand.

The Binding Update carries a 16-bit Sequence #, four flag bits and a 16-bit Lifetime in units of 4 seconds. The flags are Acknowledge (A), Home Registration (H), Link-Local Address Compatibility (L) and Key Management Mobility Capability (K). A Lifetime of zero deletes the binding.

The Binding Acknowledgement echoes the sequence number and carries a Status. Values below 128 mean the update was accepted, and values of 128 or more mean it was rejected. The Binding Error message (MH Type 7) is sent for problems such as using a Home Address option without an existing binding (status 1) or an unrecognized MH Type (status 2).

Messages can include options in a type-length-value format: Pad1, PadN, Binding Refresh Advice, Alternate Care-of Address, Nonce Indices and Binding Authorization Data. The Binding Authorization Data option, when present, MUST be the last option.
sections.plainLanguage: All the notes the devices pass around, such as telling someone your new address, asking for proof, or saying that something went wrong, use one special envelope. Each note type has its own number on the envelope.

sections.title: The Home Address Option and Type 2 Routing Header
sections.content:
Two small pieces make the care-of address invisible to higher layers. The Home Address destination option (Option Type 201, 0xC9, Option Length 16) is carried by a mobile node that is away from home. It tells the recipient the node's home address, which the recipient treats like the source address. The option can only be used when the correspondent already has a Binding Cache entry, which avoids reflection attacks.

In the other direction, the type 2 routing header lets a correspondent send directly to the care-of address. The care-of address goes into the IPv6 Destination Address, and the routing header holds the home address. It carries exactly one address (Hdr Ext Len 2, Segments Left 1), and every node processing it MUST verify that the address is its own home address, so packets cannot be forwarded elsewhere. A received type 2 routing header MUST NOT be automatically reversed.

Using a separate routing type, rather than regular source routing, lets firewalls apply different rules to Mobile IPv6 traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The home address option is like writing your permanent address on the back of the envelope, and the routing header tells the postman to deliver to your hotel first and then hand it to you by your home name.

sections.title: The Return Routability Procedure
sections.content:
A home agent and mobile node share an IPsec relationship. A correspondent node and a mobile node usually do not, and the RFC wants route optimization to work between any such pair without an authentication infrastructure. The return routability procedure does this by testing that the mobile node can really receive packets at both its claimed home address and its claimed care-of address.

The mobile node sends a Home Test Init (via the home agent) and a Care-of Test Init (directly) at the same time. Each carries a 64-bit cookie. The correspondent replies with a Home Test (via the home agent) and a Care-of Test (directly). Each carries the cookie, a nonce index and a 64-bit keygen token, which is the first 64 bits of an HMAC_SHA1 computed with the correspondent's secret 20-octet node key, an address and a nonce. The correspondent keeps no per-node state at this point.

With both tokens, the mobile node computes the binding management key Kbm = SHA-1(home keygen token | care-of keygen token). It sends a Binding Update with a Nonce Indices option and a Binding Authorization Data option, whose authenticator is the first 96 bits of an HMAC_SHA1 using Kbm. The correspondent recomputes Kbm from the nonce indices and verifies the MAC. To delete a binding, only the home keygen token is used.

Bindings created this way MUST NOT last longer than MAX_RR_BINDING_LIFETIME (420 seconds). Nonces are kept at most MAX_NONCE_LIFETIME (240 seconds) and tokens are normally usable for MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME (210 seconds). A new nonce every 30 seconds fits these limits. If return routability signaling times out after MAX_RO_FAILURE attempts, the mobile node MUST fall back to sending through the home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove you really live at both your home and your hotel, a friend sends one secret half-code to each place. You put the two halves together to make a key, and only someone who got both halves can do that.

sections.title: Protecting Home Registrations with IPsec
sections.content:
Binding Updates and Acknowledgements between a mobile node and its home agent MUST be protected by an IPsec security association for integrity and authenticity. Both sides MUST support, and SHOULD use, ESP in transport mode (RFC 4303) with a non-NULL payload authentication algorithm.

The home agent must make sure a node cannot send a Binding Update on behalf of another mobile node. It does this by checking that the home address in the update matches the security association used. The home address therefore has to be visible in these messages.

Manual configuration of security associations MUST be supported, with shared secrets that are random and unique per mobile node. Automatic key management with IKEv2 MAY be supported, as described in RFC 4877. When IKEv2 is used, the addresses carrying it must be handled carefully so that a Binding Update is not needed before the IKEv2 exchange that secures it.

Tunnels between the mobile node and the home agent are also protected by checking source addresses, and additional IPsec ESP encapsulation MAY be used. The Home Test Init and Home Test messages passing through the tunnel SHOULD use ESP in tunnel mode.
sections.plainLanguage: You and your home helper share a secret handshake. Anyone who does not know it cannot pretend to be you and tell the helper to send your mail somewhere else.

sections.title: What Home Agents and Mobile Nodes Do
sections.content:
When the mobile node moves to a new link (a layer 3 handover), it detects the move, forms a new care-of address, registers it with the home agent and then updates correspondent nodes it uses route optimization with. Movement detection uses IPv6 Neighbor Discovery: Router Discovery and Neighbor Unreachability Detection, plus hints such as the Advertisement Interval option or link-layer notifications. A mobile node should avoid a handover until it is strictly necessary.

To register, the mobile node sends a Binding Update to the home agent with the Home Registration (H) and Acknowledge (A) bits set. The packet carries a Home Address option, and an Alternate Care-of Address option MUST be included in all home registrations. Unless the home agent already has a binding for the address, it MUST perform Duplicate Address Detection on the home link before acknowledging. A failure produces status 134. Rejections use other codes, for example 131 (home registration not supported) and 132 (not home subnet).

Once registered, the home agent sends a Neighbor Advertisement for the home address, with the Override flag set and its own link-layer address, and answers Neighbor Solicitations as a proxy. It tunnels intercepted packets to the primary care-of address with IPv6 encapsulation. Packets for link-local addresses MUST NOT be tunneled.

When the node returns home, it MUST send a de-registration Binding Update with A and H set, a Lifetime of zero and its home address as the care-of address. Until then, it MUST NOT use its home address on the home link.

A mobile node that does not know its home agent can use dynamic home agent address discovery. It sends an ICMP Home Agent Address Discovery Request (type 144) to the home agents anycast address and gets one reply (type 145) listing home agent addresses. The RFC provides no security for this mechanism, which it says is designed for deployments where security is not needed. Prefix changes on the home link are delivered with Mobile Prefix Solicitation (146) and Advertisement (147) messages, which SHOULD be protected with IPsec ESP.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move, you tell your home helper your new address. The helper then collects your mail at home and forwards it. When you come back, you tell the helper to stop.

sections.title: Changes to Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 makes a few additions to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) so that home agents can be found and moves can be noticed quickly.

  • The Router Advertisement gains a Home Agent (H) bit, set by a router that is also a home agent on that link.
  • The Prefix Information option gains a Router Address (R) bit, so a router can advertise its global address. A home agent MUST include at least one such option, and this global address is needed to build the Home Agents List.
  • A new Advertisement Interval option (type 7) tells mobile nodes how often a router sends unsolicited advertisements, in milliseconds, which helps movement detection.
  • A new Home Agent Information option (type 8) carries a Home Agent Preference and a Home Agent Lifetime used to order the addresses in a discovery reply.

Fast movement detection needs faster advertisements, so routers MAY send unsolicited multicast Router Advertisements more often than before. The minimum allowed values are MinRtrAdvInterval 0.03 seconds and MaxRtrAdvInterval 0.07 seconds, giving a mean of 50 ms between advertisements. Systems MUST NOT default to these values, and the cost of frequent beacons on some wireless links should be taken into account.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers shout out "here I am" more often and with a bit more information, so a moving device can quickly notice it has arrived somewhere new and find its helper.

sections.title: Threats and Security Properties
sections.content:
Most threats concern false bindings. An attacker might claim a node is somewhere it is not, to hijack, eavesdrop or cause denial of service. A malicious node might also bind a victim's address as its own care-of address so that a correspondent floods the victim. A flow-control protocol like TCP does not necessarily prevent this, because the attacker can fake the acknowledgements. Other threats include replayed Binding Updates, reflection through the Home Address option or a routing header, forged tunnel packets, routing loops between multiple home agents, and attacks on the security mechanisms themselves.

The main defenses are mandatory reverse tunneling support, IPsec protection of home registrations, return routability for correspondent registrations, a restricted type 2 routing header, and the rule that the Home Address option is only accepted when a Binding Cache entry exists.

Return routability protects against attackers who cannot monitor the path between the home agent and the correspondent node. It does not stop attackers on that path, but the RFC notes they could mount the same attacks without Mobile IPv6. A difference is that an attacker could leave a binding behind after moving away, so bindings are limited to MAX_RR_BINDING_LIFETIME (420 seconds). The RFC also states that SHA-1 is considered secure for the foreseeable future when used as specified here.
sections.plainLanguage: The main danger is someone lying about where you are so your mail goes to them. The secret half-codes and handshakes make that very hard for anyone who is not already watching the right road.
